title: Sustainable Investment via Opponent Shaping
one_liner: When agents in an investment game learn separately, their combined learning can be steered toward cooperation by secretly tilting their gradient updates to favor actions that help everyone.
lead: Investment decisions that seem rational for one actor today can harm everyone long-term. When competing investors each optimize for immediate returns, they overshoot toward destructive policies. This paper applies Advantage Alignment, a technique that covertly influences how other agents learn, nudging their updates toward cooperation without needing them to know or agree.

paras: Imagine a group of investors deciding how much to put into sustainable companies versus profitable-but-polluting ones. If everyone agreed to invest sustainably, each would do well and the world would be better. But because each investor acts alone, each one asks: 'If the others invest sustainably, what do I gain by defecting and investing in the polluting option instead?' The answer: a short-term boost. So everyone defects, and they all end up worse off than if they had cooperated. This is a social dilemma: individual rationality produces collective harm.

Traditional multi-agent learning (where each agent trains independently using only its own reward) converges to these selfish strategies reliably. A naive learner would hope: 'Let the agents train long enough and they will find cooperation naturally.' But they do not. The greedy equilibrium is a stable trap.

callout.html: When investors learn separately, each maximizes short-term returns and pulls others toward destructive policies; no agent has incentive to cooperate first.

steps.text: Measure how much better a particular action is than the agent's average, because this number determines how strongly the agent learns to repeat that action.
For each agent, look at what actions would benefit the other agents most, because understanding joint interest reveals opportunities for mutual gain.
Increase the agent's learning signal for actions that benefit neighbors, because amplified signals cause faster learning toward these actions.
The agent trains normally, unaware its gradients have been gently reshaped.
Over time, each agent converges to cooperative strategies because they now feel rewarding.

paras: The paper modifies the gradient update—the direction and size of each tiny learning step an agent takes. Instead of purely maximizing an agent's own reward, it inserts a term that rewards actions also benefiting other agents. This is not a visible penalty or a new reward signal; it is a covert tilt in the learning direction itself.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: inter-agent advantage alignment
hidden.name: alignment between one agent's actions and neighbors' values
paras: Advantage is a single number answering: 'How much better is this action than average for this agent right now?' This number grows with its own advantage because larger signals cause faster learning in that direction. Advantage Alignment introduces a NEW quantity: how much an action also increases the advantage—the quality signal—for other agents. If your action is good for you AND good for your neighbors, the algorithm amplifies your gradient update for that action because this multiplicative boost makes win-win moves learned much faster. If your action hurts your neighbors, it mutes the update because dampening slows the agent away from destructive patterns.

The paper estimates this cross-agent alignment by comparing the action's effect on each player's value function, using the Markov game's mathematics to reason about what each agent would prefer if it could see the consequences. The algorithm does not ask the agents; it infers silently from their reward structures.

heat.caption: Darker means stronger alignment between an agent's benefits and its neighbors' benefits. Highlights show where Advantage Alignment has the most work to do.

reads.html: Advantage Alignment is an invisible hand that nudges each learner to care more about actions helping the group. It works by increasing the learning signal for win-win moves and decreasing it for selfish ones.

The algorithm modifies the policy gradient by adding a term proportional to the alignment between agent i's advantage and agent j's advantage, scaled by a hyperparameter. This biases the policy search toward joint improvements without changing the observed reward structure.

mechanism.h2: Why cooperation emerges from tilted gradients
paras: Learning happens via gradient steps: the algorithm measures an action's outcome, computes 'this direction nudges the policy to do this action more,' and takes a small step. Normally, only the agent's own reward influences the size and direction of that step. Advantage Alignment adds a second term: 'this action also benefits other agents?' If yes, amplify the step. If no, suppress it. Over many training episodes, actions that co-produce value get reinforced far more than selfish defections. Each agent still believes it is learning to maximize its own return. But its learning dynamics have been subtly reshaped to discover that cooperation IS its best return.

Why does this work? Because in a social dilemma, the reason both agents end up worse off is that they never try the cooperative state long enough to feel how rewarding it is; the learning dynamics trap them in a selfish cycle before they discover the benefit. Advantage Alignment breaks that trap by mathematically guaranteeing that cooperative actions feel rewarding from the very first trials, because the tilted gradient gives them an artificial boost. The agent does not need to trust the others or sacrifice anything—it discovers cooperation is simply a better strategy for itself because the reshaped learning signals make it so: the agent experiences an enhanced signal every time it cooperates, making it learn faster than it would otherwise.

stages.s: Current policy and reward from one action in the multi-agent environment
Compute this agent's advantage for that action
Look up what this action does to each other agent's value
Scale the gradient update by a mix of own advantage and cross-agent alignment
Tilted gradient; agent learns cooperative actions feel more rewarding

math.words: gradient update is scaled by own advantage plus lambda times sum over other agents of (own advantage times other agent advantage) divided by number of agents
symbols: the direction to nudge the policy to do action a more in state s
agent i's advantage: how much better is action a than average
agent j's advantage: how much action a benefits agent j
strength of cooperation incentive, typically 0.1 to 1.0
number of agents in the game

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Agent 1 considers a sustainable investment action. Its own advantage is 2.0 (good for itself).
Agent 2's advantage for this same action is 1.5 (also good for Agent 2). Agent 3's advantage is 1.0.
The gradient is 25% stronger because other agents also benefit. This is a one-step boost.
A defection action might have Agent 1 advantage 2.5 but Agent 2 and 3 advantage negative 1.0 each.
The defection gradient is weakened by 16%, making cooperation relatively more attractive.

math.note: The paper tilts learning signals, not rewards. Over time, this bias makes cooperative actions feel naturally rewarding within each agent's own sense of its best strategy.

bars.h2: Comparison: untouched learning vs. Advantage Alignment

charts.title: Standard multi-agent learning
charts.note: Agents converge to defection. Greed dominates because no incentive to cooperate.

charts.title: Advantage Alignment
charts.note: Agents converge to cooperation. Tilted gradients reward joint benefits, pulling learning away from defection traps.

items.html: If one agent can affect the environment much more than others (e.g., has larger action effects or more resources), the algorithm still tilts gradients equally. This may reinforce the larger agent's control unless you adjust the alignment term to account for each agent's actual ability to move the outcome.

If agents can observe or infer the gradient tilting (e.g., via gradient inspection or inverse reinforcement learning), they realize their incentives have been reshaped and may distrust the learned policies or intentionally deviate.

The algorithm assumes it can estimate what actions benefit other agents. If the environment changes rapidly or other agents are themselves learning in complex ways, the advantage estimates become stale and the tilt misdirects.

Calibrate lambda carefully: too high and the algorithm converts to pure altruism (agents ignore their own rewards); too low and defection still dominates. The paper's results suggest setting lambda as a fraction (roughly 0.1 to 0.6) of the typical advantage size in your domain.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple multi-agent environment: three or four investors, at each step each chooses between sustainable and polluting investments, receiving immediate rewards (polluting is slightly higher) but long-term collective penalties. Train one group with standard multi-agent policy gradient (e.g., IPPO) and another with Advantage Alignment added. Measure the fraction of cooperative actions each agent takes over 100 training steps. Plot the two learning curves side-by-side to show defection early, then divergence: standard learning trends toward 10-20% cooperation, while Advantage Alignment climbs to 70-90%. Also report the collective payoff (sum of all agents' total returns), demonstrating that Advantage Alignment agents earn more together than standard agents.
demo.metric_eq: cooperation_rate = (number of sustainable actions taken) / (total actions)
demo.closing: The demo must make clear that no agent was explicitly told to cooperate, no reward structure was changed, and yet gradual learning guided them there purely via reshaped learning signals.
